source_text: Libere itaque coniecto et pronuntio, quoniam si eorum aliquis his superesset diebus, videretque exstinctum disciplinae christianae decus, otiantem in omnibus liberam voluntatem, atque affectantem imputare necessitati quidquid sponte committit, vituperationem quoque operum Dei, eversionemque legis eius sub nomine inefficacis gratiae populorum auribus intimari; toto contra vos felle moveretur; perpendens etiam peccatum naturale a Manichaea non posse impietate discerni, fidem catholicam aut emendatis aut condemnatis vobis, et planius tueretur et cautius.
pass_a_gloss: I freely therefore conjecture and pronounce that if any of them survived these days, and saw the honor of Christian discipline extinguished, free will idle in all things, and affecting to impute to necessity whatever it commits spontaneously, and also a blaming of God's works and an overturning of his law under the name of an ineffective grace intimated to the ears of the peoples; he would be moved with whole bile against you; weighing also that a natural sin cannot be discerned from Manichaean impiety, he would both more plainly and more cautiously protect the catholic faith, you having been either amended or condemned.

lemmas.lexica: LS necessitas; Blaise vs free choice
Blaise Manichaeus; Julian's polemic label vs natural evil
LS naturalis; Blaise malum naturale=evil as a nature
LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS gratia=favor; Blaise grace; in iustitia definitions often 'favoritism'

pass_b_english: I therefore freely infer and pronounce that if any of them survived to the present day and saw the glory of Christian discipline extinguished, free will idle in everyone and trying to impute to necessity whatever it commits voluntarily, and disparagement of God’s works and overthrow of his law whispered into the people’s ears under the name of ineffective grace, he would be stirred against you with all his bitterness. Recognizing also that natural sin cannot be distinguished from Manichaean impiety, he would defend the catholic faith more plainly and more carefully, either correcting you or condemning you.

choices.why: Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
Julian's Manichaean charge: an evil that is a nature, not a will's act.
Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
